bibliographic.title: Adoption of AI-Driven Fraud Detection System in the Nigerian Banking Sector: An Analysis of Cost, Compliance, and Competency
bibliographic.authors: John Stephen Alaba; Shonubi Joye Ahmed; Azuikpe Patience Farida; Ologun Victor Oluwatosin
bibliographic.citation_apa: Alaba, J. S., Ahmed, S. J., Farida, A. P., & Oluwatosin, O. V. (2025). Adoption of AI-driven fraud detection system in the Nigerian banking sector: An analysis of cost, compliance, and competency. Economic Review of Nepal, 8(1), 16–33. https://doi.org/10.3126/ern.v8i1.80740

methodology.sample_description: Population of 24 licensed banks in Nigeria; purposive sampling of 5 biggest banks based on market capitalization and customer base; primary data via structured questionnaire (5-point Likert scale)
methodology.technology_context: AI-driven fraud detection systems using machine learning (supervised, unsupervised, hybrid), predictive analytics, anomaly detection, behavioural analysis, and real-time monitoring; not conversational or agentic LLM systems

eligibility.exclusion_reason: Empirical study on adoption determinants of AI/ML fraud detection in Nigerian banks; does not examine conversational AI, LLM-based systems, or conversational governance mechanisms. LLM references appear only when citing prior work in the literature review.
eligibility.decision_rationale: Although the paper addresses regulated banking, compliance, risk, and generic AI adoption, its empirical focus is fraud-detection system uptake (cost, compliance, competency) rather than governance of conversational or LLM systems. Python triage scored conversational_ai 0/3; provided text supports exclusion from the central corpus of conversational LLM governance evidence.

appraisal.notes: Clear cross-sectional survey objective and OLR estimation for adoption determinants. Purposive selection of 5 of 24 banks limits generalizability. Respondent/sample size not stated in provided excerpts. Ethics and detailed limitations not visible in supplied text.

cerqual.explanation: Methodologically coherent empirical adoption study for banking fraud-detection AI, but low relevance to conversational LLM governance because technology and governance objects differ from the review scope.

coding.theme: Adoption of AI-based fraud detection in regulated banking
coding.subtheme: Cost, compliance, and competency as adoption determinants

synthesis.main_claim: Top management support, IT infrastructure, regulatory compliance, staff competency, and perceived effectiveness accelerate adoption of AI-driven fraud detection systems in Nigerian banks, while high implementation cost discourages adoption.
synthesis.contribution: Empirical Ordered Logistic Regression evidence on organizational and regulatory factors shaping AI fraud-detection adoption in a regulated banking context.
synthesis.limitations: Purposive sample of five largest banks; respondent count and detailed limitations not provided in supplied text; no analysis of conversational AI, LLM governance, guardrails, or human oversight mechanisms for generative systems.
synthesis.use_in_review: Exclude from central conversational LLM governance synthesis; may serve only as peripheral contextual background on regulated banking AI adoption and compliance drivers if a broader regulated-sector adoption subsection is needed.
